prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
Cities should scrap their minimum parking requirements, and they should do it soon, because the rule is a subsidy for driving that nobody voted for and almost everybody pays. Parking minimums tell a developer how many spaces to build for every apartment, shop, or restaurant, usually calculated from a manual that treats suburban peak demand as a universal law. A restaurant must supply so many spaces per thousand square feet whether it sits beside a train station or at the edge of a highway, and a block of flats must provide one or two spaces per unit even if its future tenants own no cars. The effect is that the city decides how much of every lot will be given over to storing vehicles before anyone has asked what the lot is for.

The cost of that decision does not vanish. A surface space takes up roughly three hundred square feet once you count the aisles, and a space in a structured garage can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, far more underground. Developers recover that money in rents and menu prices, so a household without a car pays for parking it never uses, and since carless households skew poorer, the rule quietly taxes the people least able to bear it. Economists who have studied the question, most famously Donald Shoup, have found that the bundling of parking into everything we buy hides its true price, which is why free parking is never actually free and why drivers behave as though it were infinite.

The strongest objection is that without minimums, new buildings will leave neighbors circling for spots and the street will turn into a free-for-all. This deserves a real answer, because it is what most residents fear, and the answer is that the fear mistakes where the problem comes from. Street congestion is a pricing problem, and the remedy is to charge for curb space in places where demand is high, perhaps with the revenue returned to the neighborhood in the form of better sidewalks and lighting. Minimums do nothing to solve it, since an apartment building with a generous garage still sends its overflow guests and delivery vans to the curb. Meanwhile a developer who builds too little parking for a given market will find the units harder to rent, and the market will correct that far faster than a city council can revise a table of ratios.

Removing the requirement also does not mean parking disappears, which is a point opponents tend to skip over. Cities that have repealed their minimums, from Buffalo, which did so citywide in 2017, to Minneapolis and a growing list of others, have mostly seen developers keep building parking where customers and tenants want it. What changes is the margin. A builder on a narrow lot downtown can now decide that a ground-floor shop is worth more than six spaces, or that two extra apartments beat a ramp, and that choice, repeated across thousands of parcels, is where housing supply and walkable commerce come from. Early research on cities that have reformed suggests that new projects provide less parking than the old rules demanded but still provide plenty, which is what you would expect if the old numbers were inflated.

There is also a plain argument from housing costs. Many cities are short of homes and say so loudly, yet they keep a rule that makes each home more expensive and each lot less able to hold one. Small infill projects, such as a fourplex on a corner or a few flats above a corner shop, are often killed outright by minimums because the site cannot physically fit the required spaces, and so the modest, incremental growth that older neighborhoods once absorbed easily is simply illegal. Historic main streets that predate the automobile age would be impossible to build today for this reason alone, which should tell us something about what the rule is doing to our idea of a normal place.

The climate and fiscal cases point the same direction. Land covered in asphalt pays little property tax per acre compared with land covered in buildings, so a city that mandates parking is choosing to collect less from the very parcels it needs to support its roads and pipes. And a rule that guarantees ample storage for cars at every destination guarantees, in turn, that more people will drive to those destinations, which is difficult to square with a stated goal of cutting emissions.

None of this requires cities to be hostile to drivers. Plenty of people will always need to drive, and plenty of businesses will always want to supply parking for them, and they remain free to do so. The reform simply moves the decision from a planning code written decades ago to the owner of the land and the people who will use it, who know their circumstances better than any ratio does. If a minimum is truly necessary to make a project work, the project will include the parking without being told. If it is not, then the requirement was only ever making someone pay for something they did not want. Repeal it, price the curb honestly where demand is real, and let the land go to its best use.
